stimulus.text:
“The Congress, whenever two thirds of both Houses shall deem it necessary, shall propose Amendments to this Constitution, or, on the Application of the Legislatures of two thirds of the several States, shall call a Convention for proposing Amendments, which, in either Case, shall be valid to all Intents and Purposes, as Part of this Constitution, when ratified by the Legislatures of three fourths of the several States, or by Conventions in three fourths thereof, as the one or the other Mode of Ratification may be proposed by the Congress. . . . no State, without its Consent, shall be deprived of its equal Suffrage in the Senate.”

—Constitution of the United States, Article V, September 17, 1787
stimulus.source_note: Constitution of the United States, Article V, September 17, 1787. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus viewed before writing — Constitution of the United States, Article V, September 17, 1787, public domain.

primary_sources: Constitution of the United States, Article V (September 17, 1787)

stem: The passage protects each state’s “equal Suffrage in the Senate” from amendment without that state’s consent. What does that protection most directly show?

options.text: The framers expected the Senate to be abolished by amendment.
options.misconception: Protecting a state’s equal vote shows the Senate was meant to last, not to be abolished.

options.text: The framers wanted the Senate to grow with each new state.
options.misconception: Equal suffrage is about each state having the same two votes, not about growth.

options.text: The small states’ equal Senate voice was a bargain locked in place.
The framers believed the House would always outvote the Senate.
options.misconception: The passage says nothing about the House outvoting the Senate.

rationales.C: Background: the Senate’s equal representation was the Great Compromise that won the small states’ support, and Article V shields that bargain from later change.
rationales.A: A shield around equal suffrage guards the Senate, it does not point to abolishing it.
rationales.B: Equal suffrage means two votes per state, not a growing Senate.
rationales.D: The passage is about amending equal suffrage, not about the House outvoting the Senate.
rationales.general:
1. The passage lets most of the Constitution be amended, then carves out one exception.
2. That exception is a state’s equal vote in the Senate, which cannot be taken without the state’s own consent.
3. Background: equal Senate representation was the bargain that brought the small states into the Constitution.
4. Shielding it from amendment locks that bargain in place.
Remember: the one thing Article V shields from amendment is the bargain that made the Union possible.
